## Context resolved from project knowledge

**1. The guard and the grant it opens (the exact fix surface).**
- `scripts/pod_lifecycle.py:3472` `_guard_upload_verification_before_terminate(issue, *, skip_flag, dry_run)` — returns early on `dry_run`; returns on any unresolvable task (`FileNotFoundError` / `RuntimeError` / `ValueError`, warn-and-proceed); returns on `kind != "experiment"` (kind defaults to `"experiment"` when absent, fail-safe); then reads the LATEST `epm:upload-verification` note and returns iff it records PASS **and** carries the `outroot=` token (#2187). Two `SystemExit` refusals: PASS-without-token (3563) and no-PASS-at-all (3596).
- Call site `scripts/pod_lifecycle.py:3817` in `cmd_terminate`, ordered AFTER `_guard_keep_running_before_terminate` (3803, #1485) and BEFORE any live-API mutation.
- Passing the guard is what opens the grant: `_verified_teardown_grant(...)` (3750) wraps the `terminate_pod` loop at 3853, and `backends/kill_approval.py` `verified_teardown` (L58) / `verified_teardown_active` (L86) make `compute_kill_approved()` (L103) return True inside it (L117). So the guard's boolean IS the authorization — nothing downstream re-checks ownership. That is precisely the owner-blindness the task reports.

**2. Owner attribution has NO existing channel to read — the fix must create one.** `events.jsonl` rows carry exactly `ts, kind, version, by, note` (`task_workflow.post_event`, L5264-5310), and `by` **defaults to the literal `"unknown"`** (L5269; `scripts/task.py:1684` `p.add_argument("--by", default="unknown")`). Consequence for the plan: constraint 2 is not "read the existing attribution field" — it is "establish an attribution token on the launch side and require the PASS to match it".

## Orchestrator-side findings (union these with the critics' into the single revise round)

Raised independently of the critics (they were briefed clean, with no access to these). Numbered for the revise round to address or explicitly decline.

**OC-1 [Must-Fix candidate] — `pod.py stop` is an uncovered route to the same harm, and the plan does not even name it.** The predicate is placed only in `cmd_terminate` (plan §4.2 call site). A non-owner that concludes the owner is dead can reach substantially the same outcome via `pod.py stop --issue N`: stop preserves the volume (non-durably, #1112) but it KILLS the owner's live run — which is the harm the 2026-08-13 incident actually inflicted (an in-flight round interrupted), not merely the volume loss. The task `## Constraints` line "`pod.py stop` remains a non-substitute for verify-then-terminate (#1112)" is a durability clause, but it equally implies stop must not become the route around this new refusal. The plan's §4.2 "deliberately NOT changed" list omits stop entirely. This is also a LIVE automated path, not hypothetical: the watcher's pod-safety pass auto-STOPS (never terminates) pods at parked/terminal status, and on 2026-08-13 it logged three `pod-keep-running-skip` exemptions against these very pods — the `keep-running` tag was the only thing holding it off. Resolve as EITHER (a) bind the fence predicate in `cmd_stop` too (refuse-or-override on an unexpired non-owner fence), or (b) name it as an explicit residual in §4.2 with the reason and the compensating control.

**OC-2 [Concern] — the owner token is copyable from exactly the marker the non-owner already reads, and the owner-match WAIVER is what the copy defeats.** `owner=` is emitted on the `epm:run-launched` note (§4.3 item 1) — the same note a harvester reads to get the pod name and the HF prefixes. In the incident the harvester's PASS note enumerated prefixes "against the run's single upload call site", i.e. it was composing from the launch record. An agent that believes itself the legitimate successor may copy `owner=` forward in good faith, which silently converts the refusal into the waiver. §8's risk table covers reflexive `--force-owner-fence` use but not token copying. Two candidate resolutions for the revise round, both cheap: (i) make an UNEXPIRED fence binding regardless of owner match — the live owner's own route is then to clear its fence (`fence_until=none`) as the last step before its own teardown, which it can always do precisely because it is alive; or (ii) keep the waiver but require corroboration a non-owner cannot copy. Note (i) is strictly stronger AND removes the §8 row-2 failure mode (owner refusing its own teardown) rather than mitigating it with paired-duty prose — but it does tighten the ask-free path, so weigh it against the `## Constraints` "must not block the legitimate ask-free case" clause explicitly rather than by default.

**OC-3 [Concern] — state the operational cost of a dead owner's surviving fence.** A fence is deliberately not a heartbeat (correct — the spec forbids recency as the test), so a genuinely dead owner's fence stays binding to its deadline. The only routes past it are `--force-owner-fence` (which §4.3/§8 tell automation never to pass) or surface-for-approval, so a dead-owner pod bills until fence expiry or a human answers. That is the right conservative direction, but it is an accepted cost the plan does not state: §8's last row covers prose-durability, not this. Name it, and pair it with the mitigation the design already implies — fences are posted with the SHORTEST honest deadline and refreshed by the existing heartbeat duty, rather than posted long "to be safe".

**OC-4 [Nit] — double full-log parse per terminate.** §4.2's pseudocode calls `list_events(issue)` and then `_latest_upload_verification_note(issue)`, which calls `list_events(issue)` again (`scripts/pod_lifecycle.py:3365`). On a marker-heavy task (#2054: 577 events, ~1.6 MB) that is two full parses where one would do. Trivial in absolute time; the fix is to thread the already-read events into the note lookup, or to accept it and drop §8's "one extra read per terminate" phrasing, which currently understates it by one.
